DE-B2-01-001.notes: Reported speech in news and formal writing uses Konjunktiv I: er sei. sein is the most irregular: ich sei, du seist, er sei, wir seien. The reporter doesn't vouch for the claim.

DE-B2-01-002.notes: haben gives sie habe in Konjunktiv I: stem + -e. It's distinct from the indicative hat, which is why it's usable in reported speech.

DE-B2-01-003.notes: Modals form Konjunktiv I from the infinitive stem, without the vowel change: er könne (not kann). behaupten = claim.

DE-B2-01-004.notes: werden gives sie werde, which reports a future: the company would not cut jobs. die Firma takes the third-person singular.

DE-B2-01-005.notes: es gibt becomes es gebe in reported speech: Laut Polizei gebe es keine Verletzten. laut (according to) often introduces the source.

DE-B2-01-006.notes: The Konjunktiv I of sie haben is also haben, identical to the indicative, so Konjunktiv II hätten is used instead to mark it as reported.
DE-B2-01-006.tip: If Konjunktiv I = indicative, switch to Konjunktiv II.

DE-B2-01-007.notes: The past in Konjunktiv I uses sei / habe + participle: sie sei gewesen. Konjunktiv I has no separate simple past.

DE-B2-02-001.notes: sich lassen + infinitive means 'can be done': Das Problem lässt sich lösen. It's a common alternative to kann gelöst werden.

DE-B2-02-002.notes: sein + zu + infinitive means 'can be done': leicht zu verstehen. The same construction can also mean 'must be done' in instructions.

DE-B2-02-003.notes: In official instructions, sein + zu means 'must be done': ist einzureichen. A separable verb puts zu in the middle.

DE-B2-02-004.notes: -bar added to a verb stem gives a passive '-able': machbar (doable). It's very productive: essbar, trinkbar, erreichbar.

DE-B2-02-005.notes: lesbar (legible) is lesen + -bar. The negative is unlesbar; kaum lesbar is 'barely legible'. Not every -bar adjective is passive: dankbar (grateful) is an exception.

DE-B2-02-006.notes: man + active verb often replaces the passive in speech: Hier kann man gut essen. English uses 'you' or a passive.

DE-B2-02-007.notes: Dative verbs keep their dative in the passive and have no subject: Mir wurde geholfen. Ich wurde geholfen is wrong.
DE-B2-02-007.tip: Mir wurde geholfen, not Ich wurde geholfen.

DE-B2-02-008.notes: A subjectless passive keeps the verb in the third-person singular: wurde gratuliert. ihm (dative) stays dative.

DE-B2-02-009.notes: In the passive, durch marks a cause or means (an earthquake); von marks the agent, usually a person (the Romans).

DE-B2-02-010.notes: war + participle describes the state already reached (it was shut); wurde + participle describes the action (it got shut).

DE-B2-03-001.notes: Partizip I (infinitive + -d) means '-ing' and declines like an adjective: den schlafenden Hund. The proverb Schlafende Hunde soll man nicht wecken builds on it.
DE-B2-03-001.flag: tr: was 'Let sleeping dogs lie', the English proverb rather than a translation

DE-B2-03-002.notes: Partizip II used as an adjective means 'done, -ed': ein gekochtes Ei. After ein, the neuter accusative takes -es.

DE-B2-03-003.notes: Partizip I describes something ongoing: die steigenden Preise (rising prices). After die in the plural, -en.

DE-B2-03-004.notes: An extended attribute puts a whole phrase before the noun: der seit Jahren leer stehende Laden. English needs a relative clause.

DE-B2-03-005.notes: zu + Partizip I means 'which must / can be done': ein schwer zu lösendes Problem. It's typical of written German.

DE-B2-03-006.notes: Partizip II as an extended attribute: die im letzten Jahr gebaute Brücke. The phrase im letzten Jahr sits between article and participle.

DE-B2-03-007.notes: The perfect infinitive is participle + haben / sein: gewusst zu haben. scheinen + zu takes it to refer to the past.

DE-B2-03-008.notes: The passive infinitive is participle + werden: eingeladen zu werden. zu goes before werden. The perfect form adds worden: eingeladen worden zu sein.

DE-B2-03-009.notes: kommen takes sein, so its perfect infinitive is gekommen sein: froh, gekommen zu sein. English uses a plain past here: I'm glad I came.

DE-B2-04-001.notes: sollen can report hearsay: Er soll reich sein (he's said to be rich). The speaker passes on what others say without vouching for it.

DE-B2-04-002.notes: wollen can report the subject's own claim, often doubted: Sie will ihn nie gesehen haben. The perfect infinitive refers to the past.

DE-B2-04-003.notes: müssen can express a strong logical inference: er muss zu Hause sein (he must be). It's not about obligation here.

DE-B2-04-004.notes: dürfte (Konjunktiv II of dürfen) gives a cautious estimate: That'll probably take… It's typical of careful or formal speech.

DE-B2-04-005.notes: können expresses possibility: Das kann nicht stimmen (that can't be right). The negation makes it a firm conclusion.

DE-B2-04-006.notes: Subjective modals refer to the past with a perfect infinitive: soll geflohen sein. fliehen takes sein.

DE-B2-05-001.notes: ja (unstressed) marks something both speakers know: Das weißt du ja. It often adds a slight reproach or reminder.

DE-B2-05-002.notes: doch in an imperative urges or encourages: Komm doch mit! It softens the command into a friendly suggestion.

DE-B2-05-003.notes: mal (short for einmal) softens a request: Kannst du mal kurz helfen? Without it, the request sounds blunter.

DE-B2-05-004.notes: denn in a question signals interest or surprise: Was ist denn los? It never begins the sentence and is unstressed.

DE-B2-05-005.notes: eben marks resignation: that's just how it is. Das ist eben so is the neutral and northern form. Stressed, eben means 'just now' or 'flat, even'.

DE-B2-05-006.notes: halt means the same as eben but is southern and colloquial: Wir müssen halt warten (we'll just have to wait).
DE-B2-05-006.text: (Southern Germany / Austria) Wir müssen {{c1::halt::particle: that's just how it is (southern)}} warten.
DE-B2-05-006.flag: dup: replaced Das ist halt so (near-identical to B2-05-005 Das ist eben so)

DE-B2-05-007.notes: schon (unstressed) reassures: you'll manage, don't worry. Stressed, schon means 'already'. Here schon goes after the verb, in the middle field.
DE-B2-05-007.tr: You'll find a solution, don't worry.
DE-B2-05-007.flag: dup: replaced Keine Sorge, das klappt schon (near-identical to B1-15-003 Keine Sorge, das wird schon klappen)

DE-B2-05-008.notes: wohl expresses probability: Er ist wohl noch im Büro. It's weaker than sicher and stronger than vielleicht.

DE-B2-05-009.notes: eigentlich in a question means 'by the way, actually' and signals a change of topic or curiosity. As an ordinary adverb it means 'actually, in fact'.

DE-B2-05-010.notes: ruhig in an imperative reassures: go ahead, feel free. Komm ruhig rein = do come in. Outside imperatives, ruhig means 'calm, quiet'.

DE-B2-05-011.notes: bloß in an imperative turns it into a warning: Mach das bloß nicht! nur works the same way. In wishes, bloß means 'if only': Wäre ich bloß zu Hause!

DE-B2-05-012.notes: nur in a Konjunktiv II wish means 'if only': Wäre ich nur früher losgefahren! The verb comes first when wenn is left out.
DE-B2-05-012.text: Wäre ich {{c1::nur::particle: if only}} früher losgefahren!
DE-B2-05-012.tr: If only I'd set off earlier!
DE-B2-05-012.flag: dup: replaced Wenn er nur käme! (near-identical to B2-11-001 Wenn er doch nur käme!)

DE-B2-05-013.notes: etwa in a question signals suspicion or a hoped-for 'no': Bist du etwa krank? (you're not ill, are you?).

DE-B2-05-014.notes: aber in an exclamation intensifies: Das ist aber schön! It expresses surprise rather than contrast. Stressed or as a conjunction, aber means 'but'.

DE-B2-05-015.notes: auch in a question checks something that should be true: Hast du auch alles eingepackt? It works like an English tag question.

DE-B2-05-016.notes: vielleicht in an exclamation means 'what a…!': Das war vielleicht ein Tag! It has nothing to do with 'perhaps' here.

DE-B2-06-001.notes: indem (by doing) sends the verb to the end and describes the method. Both clauses share the subject (man).

DE-B2-06-002.notes: sodass (so that, with the result that) introduces a consequence. It can also be written so dass. so … dass splits the same idea round an adjective.

DE-B2-06-003.notes: falls (if, in case) introduces a possible condition. It's slightly more tentative than wenn. The verb goes to the end of the falls-clause.

DE-B2-06-004.notes: je nachdem (depending on) is followed by ob or a question word: je nachdem, wie das Wetter ist. It's set off by a comma.

DE-B2-06-005.notes: ohne dass (without) is used when the subject changes: Er ging, ohne dass jemand es merkte. With the same subject, ohne … zu.

DE-B2-06-006.notes: zu + adjective …, als dass + Konjunktiv II means 'too … for': zu kalt, als dass man schwimmen könnte. It's formal.

DE-B2-06-007.notes: so + adjective …, dass introduces a result: so müde, dass er einschlief. so goes before the adjective in the main clause.

DE-B2-06-008.notes: außer dass means 'except that' and sends the verb to the end. Here the reported speech keeps Konjunktiv I: er müde sei.

DE-B2-06-009.notes: während can mean 'whereas' and contrast two facts, as well as 'while' (time). The verb goes to the end either way.

DE-B2-07-001.notes: beim + nominalised infinitive means 'while doing': beim Kochen = wenn ich koche. The infinitive is capitalised as a noun.

DE-B2-07-002.notes: Nominal style replaces a clause with a noun: nach seiner Ankunft = nachdem er angekommen war. ankommen gives die Ankunft.

DE-B2-07-003.notes: durch + noun gives the means: durch regelmäßiges Üben (by practising). durch takes the accusative, and Üben is neuter.

DE-B2-07-004.notes: abfahren gives die Abfahrt: vor der Abfahrt = bevor man abfährt. Nouns from verbs in -fahren end in -fahrt.

DE-B2-07-005.notes: anmelden gives die Anmeldung: bei der Anmeldung = wenn Sie sich anmelden. -ung nouns are always feminine.

DE-B2-08-001.notes: aufgrund (due to) takes the genitive: aufgrund des Streiks. It's also written auf Grund. In speech, wegen is more common.

DE-B2-08-002.notes: angesichts (in view of) takes the genitive: angesichts der Lage. It's typical of reports and speeches.

DE-B2-08-003.notes: innerhalb (within) takes the genitive: innerhalb einer Woche. Without an article, von + dative is used: innerhalb von zwei Tagen.

DE-B2-08-004.notes: mithilfe (with the help of) takes the genitive and is also written mit Hilfe. It's often followed by von + dative when there's no article: mithilfe von Freunden.

DE-B2-08-005.notes: bezüglich (regarding) takes the genitive: bezüglich Ihrer Anfrage. It's common in business letters. hinsichtlich is a close synonym.

DE-B2-08-006.notes: gemäß (in accordance with) takes the dative and can go before or after the noun: gemäß der Hausordnung / der Hausordnung gemäß.

DE-B2-08-007.notes: zufolge (according to) takes the dative and follows its noun: dem Bericht zufolge. Before the noun it would take the genitive, which is rare.

DE-B2-08-008.notes: gegenüber in the sense 'towards, in relation to' takes the dative and follows a pronoun: mir gegenüber.

DE-B2-08-009.notes: entlang usually follows its noun with the accusative: die Straße entlang. Before the noun it takes the genitive or dative.

DE-B2-08-010.notes: dank (thanks to) takes the dative or genitive: dank seiner Hilfe. It's used for positive causes only.

DE-B2-08-011.notes: laut (according to) often takes no article: laut Wetterbericht. With an article it takes the dative or genitive.

DE-B2-08-012.notes: zuliebe (for someone's sake) takes the dative and follows the noun: dir zuliebe. It's the only common preposition that can only follow its noun.

DE-B2-08-013.notes: samt (together with) takes the dative: samt seiner Familie. It's more formal than mit. It mainly survives in samt und sonders (each and every one).

DE-B2-08-014.notes: entgegen (contrary to) takes the dative: entgegen allen Erwartungen. It can also follow the noun. In speech, gegen alle Erwartungen is more common.

DE-B2-09-001.notes: bestehen aus + dative = consist of: aus fünf Personen. The same verb with auf means 'insist on'. The team is the subject, so the verb is singular.
DE-B2-09-001.tip: bestehen aus (consist of) vs bestehen auf (insist on).

DE-B2-09-002.notes: bestehen auf + dative = insist on: auf einer Entschuldigung. Unusually, auf here takes the dative, not the accusative.

DE-B2-09-003.notes: abhängen von + dative = depend on. The prefix ab goes to the end: Das hängt von dir ab. The question form is Wovon hängt das ab?

DE-B2-09-004.notes: sich verlassen auf + accusative = rely on. Here auf ihn is fronted for emphasis. The noun is der Verlass: Auf ihn ist Verlass.

DE-B2-09-005.notes: sich bewerben um + accusative = apply for (a job); bei + dative = with (a company). The noun is die Bewerbung (application).

DE-B2-09-006.notes: verzichten auf + accusative = do without, give up: auf Kaffee verzichten. The noun is der Verzicht. The verb goes to the end after the modal kann.

DE-B2-09-007.notes: sich gewöhnen an + accusative = get used to. The Perfekt uses haben: habe mich gewöhnt. The adjective is gewöhnt an or gewohnt (+ accusative).

DE-B2-09-008.notes: sich beschweren über + accusative = complain about; bei + dative = complain to. Both appear here. The noun is die Beschwerde (complaint).

DE-B2-10-001.notes: eine Entscheidung treffen = make a decision. treffen is the fixed verb; machen would be a calque from English.

DE-B2-10-002.notes: zur Verfügung stellen = make available, provide. stellen splits from its phrase: stellt … zur Verfügung.

DE-B2-10-003.notes: nicht in Frage kommen = be out of the question. Also written infrage. Positively, in Frage kommen means 'be an option'.

DE-B2-10-004.notes: Bescheid sagen / geben = let someone know. It's neutral and very common in speech. The noun Bescheid is always used without an article here.

DE-B2-10-005.notes: in Kraft treten = come into force. treten has e → i: es tritt. The Perfekt is ist in Kraft getreten.

DE-B2-10-006.notes: zum Ausdruck bringen = express. The phrase is more formal than ausdrücken. bringen goes into the Präteritum here: brachte.

DE-B2-10-007.notes: in Anspruch nehmen = take up (time); also make use of (a service). Anspruch also means 'claim, entitlement'.

DE-B2-11-001.notes: Strong verbs have their own Konjunktiv II: Präteritum stem + umlaut + -e: kam → käme. Wenn … doch nur expresses a wish.

DE-B2-11-002.notes: wissen → wüsste is used freely in speech: Ich wüsste gern… (I'd like to know). würde wissen is avoided.

DE-B2-11-003.notes: geben → gäbe: wenn es keine Autos gäbe. es gibt / gäbe is one of the strong forms still common in speech.

DE-B2-11-004.notes: gehen → ginge. In speech würde gehen is also common, but es ginge is idiomatic in this phrase. The main clause and the condition both use Konjunktiv II.
DE-B2-11-004.text: Es {{c1::ginge::gehen · Konjunktiv II, es}} schneller, wenn du mir helfen würdest.
DE-B2-11-004.flag: text: wenn du hilfst mixed the indicative with a Konjunktiv II main clause; changed to wenn du mir helfen würdest

DE-B2-11-005.notes: With a modal, the past Konjunktiv II is hätte + infinitive + modal infinitive: hätte kommen sollen (should have come).

DE-B2-11-006.notes: hättest … anrufen können = could have called. The modal stays an infinitive, not gekonnt, and goes last. It often carries a mild reproach.

DE-B2-11-007.notes: The condition can be a phrase: ohne dich (= wenn du nicht da wärst). The main clause still uses Konjunktiv II: wäre.

DE-B2-11-008.notes: fast + Konjunktiv II past means 'nearly happened': Fast wäre ich gestürzt. The Konjunktiv marks it as not real.

DE-B2-11-009.notes: bei + noun can replace a wenn-clause: bei schönem Wetter (= wenn das Wetter schön wäre). The verb is Konjunktiv II.

DE-B2-11-010.notes: With a double infinitive in a subordinate clause, the auxiliary goes before the two infinitives: dass er hat arbeiten müssen.

DE-B2-11-011.notes: The same rule with lassen: ob ich das Auto habe reparieren lassen. It's an exception to verb-final order.

DE-B2-12-001.notes: es fills the first position and points forward to the dass-clause: Es freut mich, dass… It disappears if the clause comes first.

DE-B2-12-002.notes: es fills the first position in an impersonal passive: Es wurde getanzt. If something else comes first, es drops: Gestern wurde getanzt.

DE-B2-12-003.notes: es can stand in for a subject that comes later: Es kamen viele Leute. The verb agrees with viele Leute (plural).

DE-B2-12-004.notes: man has no oblique forms of its own; einen serves as its accusative: So etwas freut einen. The nominative is still man.

DE-B2-12-005.notes: einem is the dative of man: Das kann einem passieren. passieren takes the dative. schon mal softens it: it can happen.

DE-B2-13-001.notes: Futur II (werden + participle + haben / sein) mostly expresses an assumption about the past: Er wird den Zug verpasst haben.

DE-B2-13-002.notes: Futur II can also mean 'will have done by then': Bis morgen werde ich das Buch gelesen haben. In speech, the Perfekt with bis morgen is more common.

DE-B2-13-003.notes: gehen takes sein, so Futur II ends in gegangen sein: Sie wird schon gegangen sein. schon adds 'surely, probably'.

DE-B2-14-001.notes: alle is a der-word, so the following adjective takes the weak plural -en: alle neuen Studenten. The same goes for beide, keine and the plural possessives.

DE-B2-14-002.notes: viele is not a der-word, so the adjective takes the strong plural -e: viele neue Studenten. The same goes for mehrere, wenige and einige.

DE-B2-14-003.notes: After die beiden, the adjective takes -en, like after die: die beiden jungen Frauen. Without die, beide works like alle: beide jungen Frauen.

DE-B2-14-004.notes: einige (some) works like viele: the adjective takes the strong -e: einige gute Bücher. In the genitive plural it would be einiger guter Bücher.

DE-B2-14-005.notes: Numbers are not der-words, so the adjective takes strong endings: drei kleine Kinder. With an article, it would be die drei kleinen Kinder.

DE-B2-15-001.notes: haben + zu + infinitive means 'have to, must': Du hast hier nichts zu sagen (you have no say). It sounds authoritarian.

DE-B2-15-002.notes: scheinen + zu = seem to: Er scheint müde zu sein. Without zu it isn't correct. The perfect infinitive gives the past: Er scheint es gewusst zu haben.

DE-B2-15-003.notes: drohen + zu = threaten to, be in danger of: droht einzustürzen. A separable verb puts zu in the middle.

DE-B2-15-004.notes: pflegen + zu = be in the habit of. It's formal and somewhat literary. In speech, normalerweise or meistens is used instead.

DE-B2-16-001.notes: Name is an irregular n-noun: dem Namen, but the genitive takes -ns: des Namens. dem Namen nach = by name.

DE-B2-16-002.notes: The genitive of Name is Namens, with both -n and -s. Gedanke, Buchstabe, Glaube and Wille behave the same way.

DE-B2-16-003.notes: Herz is neuter and irregular: dem Herzen, des Herzens, but das Herz in the accusative. von Herzen = sincerely.

DE-B2-16-004.notes: Gedanke takes -n in the dative: mit dem Gedanken. sich mit etwas anfreunden = get used to something.

DE-B2-16-005.notes: Präsident is a regular n-noun: den Präsidenten. Most masculine nouns in -ent are n-nouns. The feminine is Präsidentin, with regular endings.

DE-B2-16-006.notes: Mensch is an n-noun: keinen Menschen. keinen Menschen kennen = not know a soul. The plural is die Menschen.

DE-B2-16-007.notes: derselbe (the very same) declines in both parts: in demselben Haus. der gleiche means an identical but separate one.
DE-B2-16-007.tip: derselbe = the very same; der gleiche = an identical one.

DE-B2-16-008.notes: derjenige / diejenigen (the one(s) who) points forward to a relative clause. Both parts decline. In speech, die, die … or alle, die … is more common.

DE-B2-16-009.notes: Naming both forms (Kolleginnen und Kollegen) is the established inclusive address in letters and speeches.

DE-B2-16-010.notes: Participle nouns such as die Studierenden are gender-neutral in the plural and widely used at universities.
DE-B2-16-010.text: Die {{c1::Studierenden::students (gender-neutral participle noun)}} protestieren gegen die Gebühren.
DE-B2-16-010.tr: The students are protesting against the fees.
DE-B2-16-010.flag: dup: replaced Alle Studierenden müssen sich anmelden (near-identical to B2-14-001 Alle neuen Studenten müssen sich anmelden)

DE-B2-16-011.notes: Decades are written as one word: die Neunzigerjahre, or 90er-Jahre. in den … takes the dative plural.

DE-B2-17-001.notes: Separable umfahren (stress on um) means knock down: hat umgefahren, with ge- in the middle. The stress decides the meaning.

DE-B2-17-002.notes: Inseparable umfahren (stress on fahren) means drive round: hat umfahren, with no ge-. The noun is die Umfahrung (Austrian: bypass).

DE-B2-17-003.notes: Inseparable übersetzen (stress on setzen) means translate: ich übersetze, participle übersetzt. The noun is die Übersetzung.

DE-B2-17-004.notes: Separable übersetzen (stress on über) means ferry across: setzt … über. The literal meaning goes with the separable form.

DE-B2-17-005.notes: Inseparable durchschauen means see through (a person): durchschaut, without ge-. Separable durchschauen means look through.

DE-B2-17-006.notes: erschrecken is strong when it means 'be startled' (erschrak) and weak when it means 'startle someone' (erschreckte).

DE-B2-17-007.notes: schaffen is strong for 'create' (schuf, geschaffen) and weak for 'manage' (schaffte, geschafft). In speech, geschafft (managed) is far more common.

DE-B2-17-008.notes: wiegen is strong for 'weigh' (wog, gewogen) and weak for 'rock' (wiegte, gewiegt). Weighing oneself is sich wiegen: Ich wiege mich.

DE-B2-18-001.notes: After etwas, nichts or alles, a preposition + relative becomes wo(r)-: etwas, worüber… (nachdenken über).

DE-B2-18-002.notes: alles, wofür… uses wofür because arbeiten takes für. wo + für needs no r. The participle gearbeitet is followed by habe in the subordinate clause.

DE-B2-18-003.notes: wer with no antecedent means 'whoever': Wer zu spät kommt, muss draußen warten. The main clause can add der.

DE-B2-18-004.notes: was with no antecedent means 'what, that which': Was du sagst, stimmt nicht. In colloquial speech, das, was du sagst is also heard.
